Rock Excavation

Sandstone and shale, broken with the right attachment

Rock excavation using hammers, rippers and the attachment the ground actually calls for. Sandstone across the coastal side of Sydney, shale across the Cumberland Plain, and a weathered profile above both that often rips where the rock beneath it will not. The strongest geographic association we have is the Northern Beaches.

Before anything starts

Six things have to be settled first, and not all of them are ours

Most jobs that run late run late on this list rather than on the work itself. Each line says who owns it.

  1. 01

    Geotechnical report

    Who You, through a consultant

    Rock level and strength. This is the single piece of information that turns a rate into a price on a rock job.

  2. 02

    Extent and levels

    Who You, through your surveyor or engineer

    How much rock is actually in the design volume, as opposed to how much is on the block.

  3. 03

    Neighbour notification and dilapidation

    Who You

    Hammering is felt next door. A dilapidation report before, and a conversation before that, protects both sides.

  4. 04

    Approved working hours

    Who You or your certifier

    Hammer work is usually the noisiest thing that will happen on the site, and hours are commonly a condition.

  5. 05

    Access for the machine that can do it

    Who Both of us

    A hammer needs a machine with the weight to hold it. On a tight block that may not be the machine that fits.

  6. 06

    Spoil destination

    Who Max

    Clean excavated sandstone is a useful material rather than a waste, where it can be kept clean.

The detail

What decides whether rock rips or has to be hammered

  • What the rock is. Hawkesbury Sandstone is strong and generally needs a hammer once you are past the weathered crust. Shale often rips, because the bedding does part of the work.
  • How weathered it is. The top of a rock profile is usually far softer than the rock beneath, and a dig can start easily and then stop.
  • Which direction the bedding runs. A ripper working with the bedding is efficient. Working across it is not.
  • The machine weight. A hammer needs a carrier heavy enough to hold it down. The machine that fits the block may not be the machine that breaks the rock.
  • How close the neighbours are. Hammer work transmits. On a tight block the method is often chosen around the adjoining structure rather than around the rock.
  • Whether the rock is wanted. Clean sandstone has value. Mixing it with soil and debris turns a useful material into a disposal cost.

Before you book

What people ask about this one

How do you price rock nobody has measured?
By the cubic metre at a rate agreed before we start. The strip, the access and the cartage come from a site visit; the rock volume comes from what is actually encountered. Quoting a fixed figure for an unmeasured quantity is a guess that somebody pays for.
Do you blast?
No. Hammers, rippers and the right attachment. Blasting in a Sydney residential context is rarely practical and is not something we offer.
How loud is it, and for how long?
A hydraulic hammer in sandstone is the loudest thing that will happen on most residential sites. We work within the approved hours and will tell you which days will be worst so you can let the neighbours know.
Can rock be ripped instead of hammered?
Where the ground allows it, yes, and it is faster and quieter. Shale and weathered profiles often rip. Competent sandstone generally does not.
What happens to the rock?
Clean excavated sandstone is a useful material and goes somewhere it can be used rather than to landfill, provided it has been kept separate from soil and debris.
